source.title: Shade: Information-Based Regularization for Deep Learning
source.authors: Michael Blot; Thomas Robert; N. Thomé; M. Cord

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices.
record.tranche_reason: Tests the effect of a new explicit regularizer on held-out image classification accuracy, including varied training-set sizes and a large-scale ImageNet setting. It does not test the listed memorization, optimizer, batch-size, architecture-bias, or generalization-measure claims directly.
record.gate_note: Rows record the paper's own reported test-set accuracies for regularization comparisons, SHADE fine-tuning, and training-set-size conditions. The binary-activation experiment changes an activation and fine-tunes the upper layers, but does not test a listed claim version. Excluded cited findings are not this study's results. Validation accuracies used to tune regularization weights are not separate results.
record.test_reason: Table 1 tests V6 by comparing validation-tuned dropout with no regularization, and bears on V3 by reporting substantially higher accuracy for convolutional networks than for an MLP under the same CIFAR-10 preprocessing and momentum-SGD protocol. Training accuracy is unnecessary for these test-error comparisons. The SHADE experiments themselves do not test a listed version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate: the authors conclude that SHADE improves on weight decay and dropout across the tested CIFAR-10 architectures, scales to ImageNet, and benefits limited-data training. Their characterization of improvements as significant is not accompanied by uncertainty estimates or statistical tests; the ImageNet comparison also lacks a matched fine-tuning control without SHADE.
record.recipe_differences: Introduces and evaluates SHADE, an explicit information-based regularizer; CIFAR-10 experiments use momentum SGD, while MNIST-M uses Adam. Does not reproduce the original interventions in the listed versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and training-set size; reported SHADE benefits are larger with limited training samples. CIFAR-10 results vary by architecture and regularization method.

fits_no_version.finding: SHADE raises CIFAR-10 accuracy over no regularization in all four architectures and has the highest reported accuracy in each architecture.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SHADE improves test accuracy in these tested CIFAR-10 recipes.

fits_no_version.finding: WELDON accuracy rises from 78.51% to 80.14% top-1 and from 94.65% to 95.35% top-5 after SHADE fine-tuning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The reported WELDON checkpoint improves after SHADE fine-tuning; the isolated contribution of SHADE requires a matched fine-tuning control.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors report SHADE gains of 10–15 percentage points on small MNIST-M subsets and six points with 4,000 CIFAR-10 examples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SHADE has larger benefits with limited training data in the tested settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Selected-layer activation binarization followed by upper-layer fine-tuning generally preserves much of the original accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Binary activations can retain much of the classification information used by these networks after upper-layer adaptation.

record.problems: The paper reports test accuracy but not training accuracy, so the training-test gap cannot be assessed. No uncertainty estimates are stated. Figure 2 values are plotted without exact values in the text. Appendix A's CIFAR-10 learning-rate and decay entries are blank in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: None; all separately reported numeric test accuracies and plotted training-size conditions were retained.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and chance-level held-out accuracy under matched natural-label and random-label recipes.
Width sweeps, interpolation threshold, and test error beyond zero training error.

Isolating local connectivity from other architectural differences; learning sparse local connections; convolutional initialization of fully connected networks. The architecture comparisons do not match parameter counts.
Matched optimizer comparisons and tuning-budget effects.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove penalties.
Dropout on very small datasets, excessive dropout causing underfitting, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation. The low-data experiments vary SHADE, not dropout.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization-gap correlations, and comparisons with other measures.
Memorization-based example removal compared with random removal.

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source for V3 or V6. R11 and R15 require version-specific states: absent for a meaningful dropout benefit under the authors' characterization, observed for convolutional superiority over the MLP. The single state field cannot express both. Table 1 values should take precedence over minor arithmetic discrepancies in the prose.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and held-out natural-label performance under the same architectures and recipes.
Width sweep beyond interpolation and resulting test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons and the role of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer generalization under differing tuning budgets.
Large versus small batch generalization under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout itself is compared with other regularizers, but the study does not test the stated dropout-regime claims or jointly remove dropout and weight decay with augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the train-test gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the effect on held-out accuracy.
